props.title: Ghost Town
props.initialSlug: Gothic ghost story as romantic comedy

sections.content: Ghost Town brilliantly reinvents the supernatural comedy genre pioneered by Ghost (1990) through Ricky Gervais's pitch-perfect portrayal of misanthropic dentist Bertram Pincus. The film cleverly subverts expectations by making its ghost-seeing protagonist actively despise helping others, unlike the more willing mediums seen in films like The Sixth Sense (1999) or Just Like Heaven (2005). Director David Koepp, better known for scripting blockbusters like Jurassic Park (1993), brings a surprisingly delicate touch to this romantic comedy.

sections.content: What sets Ghost Town apart is its grounding in genuine human emotion rather than supernatural spectacle. Like Truly Madly Deeply (1990) and The Others (2001), it uses its ghostly premise to explore grief, loneliness, and the difficulty of human connection. Téa Leoni and Greg Kinnear provide stellar support, with their characters' complex relationship avoiding typical romantic comedy clichés while delivering genuine emotional payoff.

The film's New York setting becomes almost a character itself, reminiscent of how Manhattan (1979) used the city to frame its romantic story. The ghosts populating the streets create a parallel city of the dead, each with unfinished business that reflects universal human regrets and desires. This approach elevates the film beyond simple comedy into a meditation on what it means to truly live. SUBHEAD: Modern Ghost Romance Evolution

sections.content: Ghost Town represents a significant evolution in supernatural romance, building on foundations laid by films like Always (1989) and City of Angels (1998). Where earlier films often relied on tragic love stories, this film uses its supernatural elements to facilitate personal growth and redemption. The dentist's journey from isolation to engagement with life mirrors similar character arcs in films like As Good as It Gets (1997), but with the added dimension of spiritual intervention.
